videos.title: How We Build Effective Agents: Barry Zhang, Anthropic
videos.result: Start with an environment, tools, and a prompt. Add complexity only after the basic loop works.
plan: Define the environment, available tools, goals, and stopping conditions.
Start with one model–tool loop. Inspect the feedback each tool returns.
Test representative tasks before adding routing, memory, or parallel agents.

evidence.quote: They're models using tools in a loop.
any complexity up front is really going to kill iteration speed.

videos.coverage: Selected search passages about simplicity, tools, and agent loops; not the full talk.

videos.title: Arrakis: How To Build An AI Sandbox From Scratch - Abhishek Bhardwaj, OpenAI
videos.result: Compare shared-kernel containers with microVM isolation. Include GPU needs and snapshot/restore—not just startup speed.
plan: Define what untrusted code must not access: host data, credentials, and network destinations.
Compare isolation boundaries, GPU support, and I/O costs for your workload.
Prototype snapshot, execute, and restore. Verify state recovery and cleanup with a failing task.

evidence.quote: each VM has its own guest user space and guest kernel.
you do get GPU access more easily in G Visor and containers versus like microVMs

videos.coverage: Selected passages on isolation, security trade-offs, and snapshot/restore. The search bundle was budget-limited; not a full architecture review.

videos.title: Context Engineering for AI Agents with LangChain and Manus
videos.result: Keep bulky tool results in files and their paths in context. Recover the originals instead of trusting a lossy summary.
plan: Persist bulky results; keep paths so the agent can retrieve the originals.
Compact older calls first. Retain recent complete tool examples.
Evaluate task success and missing-field errors before turning to lossy summaries.

evidence.quote: drop the super long content field and just keep the path.
we still like keep the last few tool calls and tool results in full detail

videos.title: Patrick Collison — Why Silicon Valley's most talented should leave
videos.result: Write down the decision and its reasoning. Future teammates inherit the context, not another meeting.
plan: Pick a recurring decision your team keeps reopening.
Write a one-page note: options, rationale, owner, and a revisit trigger.
Ask someone outside the meeting to explain the decision using only that note.

evidence.quote: I and lots of people write things in order to organize one's own thoughts.

videos.title: Thrive Capital’s Miles Grimshaw: Why Software Moats Just Disappeared
videos.result: Separate features a rival can rebuild from the customer relationships they still have to earn.
plan: List the features a well-funded rival could recreate with today’s tools.
Identify customers and ecosystem relationships that a replica would still have to win.
Try one customer-specific feature; check whether customers value it enough to stay.

evidence.quote: Might not have any residents yet, but you can build that city.
companies now should say yes to like one customer's needed feature.

videos.title: How Brian Chesky Is Redesigning Airbnb for the AI Era
videos.byline: Brian Chesky · Invest Like the Best
videos.result: Imagine an absurdly great first experience. Work backwards to one improvement you can actually deliver.
plan: Pick one moment: a customer’s first successful use.
Sketch a five-star, seven-star, and absurd eleven-star version.
Work backwards to one affordable delight. Test it with a customer before scaling.

evidence.quote: you keep pushing to go so absurd to 10 stars that suddenly six or seven stars doesn't seem crazy at all.
